etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Yojijukugo (四(よ)字(じ)熟(じゅく)語(ご)), from 一所懸命(いっしょけんめい) (isshokenmei), which referred to samurais risking their life to defend the territory inherited from ancestors.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese 七 (nana), ultimately from Proto-Japonic *nana.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 七 (MC tshit). Compare Hokkien 七 (chhit), Hakka 七 (chhit).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shortening from nana above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Mandarin 七 (qī).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The regular 下一段活用 (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) shift of Old Japanese and Classical Japanese verb 並ぶ (narabu, “to line up (intransitive); to line something up (transitive)”).
The root verb narabu appears in Old Japanese, at least as early as the Man'yōshū of 759 CE.
Probably reflecting the same nara root as verb 均す・平す (narasu, “to flatten something out, to line something up horizontally”) + ぶ (bu, suffix attaching to nouns and adjectives to indicate ongoing state or likeness). If so, probably deriving ultimately from verb 成る・為る・生る (naru, “to come into being; to become”), 慣る・馴る・狎る・熟る (naru, “to become normal, to become regular, to become fitting”, classical form of modern なれる (nareru)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 入り (iri, “entry, going in”) + 口 (kuchi, “mouth; opening”). The kuchi changes to guchi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 動物 (duwng^X mjut)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 半 (MC panH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Attested in the Man'yōshū completed in 759.
In turn, derived from verb 旧(ふ)る (furu, “to age, to become older”, said of both things and people) + し (-shi, Old and Classical Japanese adjective-forming suffix), with the verb itself also attested in the Man'yōshū.
The modern form 古(ふる)い (furui) emerged as a regular shift from 古(ふる)き (furuki), the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) of classical adjective 古(ふる)し (furushi).
⟨puruki₁⟩ → */puruki/ → /furui/

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/opoki/ → /oɸoki/ → /oɸokiki/ → /owokiː/ → /oːkiː/
Appears in the Muromachi period, 1337 to 1573 CE.
From older adjective 大(おお)き (ōki, ancient reading opoki), derived as the attributive form ōki (ancient opoki) of cognate adjective ōshi (ancient oposi; attributive opoki appearing already in the Man'yōshū of 759 CE, meaning both “large” or “many”, spelled as 多(おお)し (ōshi) or 大(おお)し (ōshi), modern Japanese 多(おお)い (ōi, “many”)), in turn derived from Old Japanese adjective opo (“indistinct; of uncertain size, shape, or amount”; read as ō in modern Japanese, spelled as 凡 or 大).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Probably from Middle Chinese compound 失禮 /失礼 (syit lej^X, literally “lose, loss + propriety”). Compare modern Hokkien 失禮 /失礼 (sit-lé).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From classical 安(やす)し (yasushi), from Old Japanese. First appears in the Kojiki of 712 CE as 夜須（久） (yasu(ku)). In turn from Proto-Japonic *yasu. Cognate with 休(やす)む (yasumu, “to rest”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Possibly related to 少し (sukoshi). Possibly cognate with the ku part in 幾 (iku).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 年 (nen, “year”). Compare modern Mandarin reading nián, Hakka ngièn, Cantonese nin⁴.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨to₂si⟩ → /tosi/ → /toɕi/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *təsi. Originally referred to grain, particularly rice, and by extension, the year's harvest.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/to₂se/ → /tose/
From Old Japanese. Likely a shift in pronunciation from 年(とし) (toshi).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 弱し (*yo₁wasi), from Proto-Japonic *yowa-.
Although not phonetically attested in Old Japanese texts in man'yōgana, the name of a king varies between 目弱王 in the Kojiki and 眉輪王, read as mayo₁wa-WAU in the Nihon Shoki.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨padukasiki₁⟩ → /padukasikʲi/ → /ɸadukaɕiki/ → /ɸadukaɕiː/ → /ɸad͡zukaɕiː/ → /hazukaɕi.i/
From Old Japanese. First cited to the Man'yōshū of circa 759 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From classical わろし (waroshi). Compare まるい (marui) < まろし (maroshi).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/rjokau/ → /rjokɔː/ → /rjokoː/
From Middle Chinese compound 旅行 (ljo^X hæng, literally “to travel + to walk”). Compare modern Hakka reading lî-hàng, Min Nan readings lí-hêng, lú-hêng.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the noun 雲(くも) (kumo, “cloud”) + る (-ru, verb suffix).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 毎 (mai-, “each; every”) + 日 (nichi, jitsu, “day”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨mi₁du⟩ → */mʲidu/ → /mid͡zu/ → /mizu/
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. In turn, from Proto-Japonic *mentu. Ryukyuan cognates support the existence of the first vowel having an initial mid vowel.
Possibly cognate with 瑞 (mizu, “freshness, youth”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨mi₁⟩ → */mʲi/ → /mi/
From Old Japanese.
Typically found in compounds.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ɕuwi/ → */suwi/ → /sui/
From Middle Chinese 水 (MC sywijX).
Compare modern Mandarin 水 (shuǐ), modern Hakka 水 (súi).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨mopi₁⟩ → */mopʲi/ → /moɸi/ → /mowi/ → /moi/
From Old Japanese. Via metonymy from the word 椀, 盌 (moi, “bowl”), from the meaning of “that which goes in the 椀, 盌 (moi, “bowl”)”. Compare the development of modern English cuppa, where the word for the container is similarly used to refer to the contents.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the conjunctive form of the verb 決(けっ)する (kessuru, “to decide”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 點 (MC temX, “point”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨mo₂no₂⟩ → ⟨mono₂⟩ → /mono/
From Old Japanese. Attested in the Kojiki. Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *mənə.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/mono/ → /mon/
Shift from mono above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 物 (MC mjut). Compare Hokkien 物 (bu̍t).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Early Middle Japanese adjective 狭(せま)し (semashi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in き (ki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of い (i). Originally 狭し (sebashi); underwent a sound change from /b/ to /m/, similar to 寂しい (sabishii, samishii, “lonely, desolate”), 頭 (tsuburi, tsumuri, “head”), and 煙 (keburi, kemuri, “smoke”).
Cognate with 攻(せ)める (semeru), 責(せ)める (semeru), 迫(せま)る (semaru), 狭(せば)める (sebameru), and 狭(せば)まる (sebamaru), and 窄(すば)る (subaru, “to become narrow”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨siro₁⟩ → */sirʷo/ → /ɕiro/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *siro.
The standalone apophonic form of shira below.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨sira⟩ → /ɕira/
From Old Japanese. The 被(ひ)覆(ふく)形(けい) (hifukukei, “bound form”) of 白(しろ) (shiro), mostly used in compounds.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 白 (MC baek).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. From Proto-Japonic *miru. Cognate with 目(め) (me, “eye”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *oya. Cognate with or derived from Old Japanese verb 老ゆ (oyu, “to become old”, modern 老いる oiru), from the idea of one's elders.
First cited in the Kojiki of 712.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 親 (MC tshin).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *panas-.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 話 (MC hwaejH). Irregular progression possibly influenced by modern Mandarin reading huà.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Attested from the 19th century. Sound shift from slightly earlier 赤坊 (akabō), from 赤 (aka, “red”) + 坊 (-bō, “little”). Compare 赤ちゃん (aka-chan) and 赤子 (akago), both of which also allude to the reddish complexion of a newborn.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Probably from Old Japanese. First cited in the ten-volume Wamyō Ruijushō of 934 CE.
Unknown derivation. Theories include:
* Compound of 天(あ) (a, “heaven, sky”) + 玉(たま) (tama, “ball”). This is problematic phonetically, as 天 appears historically as ama or ame, not as just a.
* Compound of 当(あ)て (ate, “putting something in contact”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 当(あ)てる (ateru, “to hit”)) + 間(ま) (ma, “space, gap”), referring to the head as a moxibustion point. This is also problematic phonetically, as the shift from ate to ata necessitates a change in meaning of the underlying verb. This is also problematic semantically, as the term 間(ま) (ma) term refers more specifically to a gap or space.
* Compound of 貴(あて) (ate, “noble”) + 間(ま) (ma, “space”), referring to the most important part of the body. However, the use of 間(ま) (ma) in this way is again problematic. Moreover, 貴(あて) (ate, “noble”) appears in The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter dating to the 900s CE, while 頭(あたま) (atama) with a sense of fontanelle appears in the Wamyō Ruijushō dated 938 CE, leaving insufficient time for either the semantic or phonetic drift required.
Historically, this term first appears with a sense of fontanelle, in reference to the soft place on the top of an infant's head where the bones of the skull have not yet fused. As such, a more likely derivation might be as a compound of 当(あ)た (ata, “not quite touching, not quite in contact”, 未(み)然(ぜん)形(けい) (mizenkei, “irrealis form”) of classical verb 当(あ)つ (atsu) and root of modern 当(あ)たる (ataru, “to touch, to come into contact”)) + 間(ま) (ma, “space, gap, opening”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Found as a standalone noun in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE, and as a counter in the Kojiki, dating to 712 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Cognate with and shift in meaning from かぶり (kaburi, “covering; hat, crown”), spelled in kanji as 被り or 冠.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese; first attested in the Kojiki (712), with the spelling 加夫, in spite that the Nihon Kokugo Daijiten lists the first attestation as from the late Muromachi period.
Cognate with 株(かぶ) (kabu, “stump; root”), from a general sense of lump.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Cognate with 粒 (tsubu, “round thing”, such as a grain), 禿ぶ (tsubu, “to go bald”, from the idea of one's head becoming round), 円ら (tsubura, “round”, adjective), 潰れる (tsubureru, “to become rounded, as from wear and tear, or from crushing”).
Some sources derive this as a shift from 円ら (tsubura, “round”, adjective). However, the phonology and semantics for this do not fit (changing /a/ to /i/, and repurposing the adjectivizing suffix ら to instead form a noun). The modern verb tsubureru had the form tsuburu in older stages of the language. The tsuburi reading for 頭 may more likely represent a nominalization derived from this older verb, following normal patterns for creating nouns from verbs.
Compare Okinawan ちぶる (chiburu, “head”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From tsuburi above. Bilabial plosive /b/ becomes bilabial nasal /m/.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shortened from tsumuri above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
*/kamipe/ → */kampe/ → /kaube/ → /kɔːbe/ → /koːbe/
Compound of either 上 (kami, “upper”) or 髪 (kami, “hair”) (likely cognates), with either 部 (be, “part, portion”) or 辺・方 (pe, “area; direction”).
Listed in one resource as possibly an alteration from 頭 (kabu, “head”) + 上 (upe, “up”, Old Japanese reading).
This reading is listed in some sources as attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720. However, this is based on traditional ruby glosses of the ideogrammatic spelling, and the glosses are from younger manuscripts.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Contraction of ど (do-, “super-”, often used ironically as a derogatory prefix) + 頭 (atama, “head”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/du/ → /d͡zu/ → /zu/
From Middle Chinese 頭 (MC duw). The goon reading, so likely an earlier borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 頭 (MC duw). The kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing. The shift from initial /d/ to voiceless /t/ is due to influence or reborrowing from a later stage of the Chinese language. Compare modern Mandarin reading tóu, Cantonese tau⁴, Min Nan tao⁵.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 飛行(ひこう) (hikō, “aviation”) + 場(じょう) (-jō, “place”)
